newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heat ends higher on forecasts for cold.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heat ends higher on forecasts for cold.

text.p: NYMEX heating oil ended higher Tuesday as demand was seen increasing on forecasts for sub-normal temperatures in the U.S. Northeast and Midwest at a time when inventories are low.
"We may be seeing concerned buying by consumers who feel they need to load up in case there is a shortage," said A.G. Edwards analyst Bill O'Grady.

December heating oil ended 1.83 cents up at 73.68 cents a gallon. Heating oil's rally paced gains in the rest of the oil complex. Dec crude ended up 61 cents at $24.49 a barrel. Dec gasoline ended up 1.62 cents at 67.39 cents a gallon.

"It's definitely the cold weather behind this," said Rita Beale, analyst with Fimat USA Futures in Houston. Beale said cold weather on both sides of the Atlantic spurred gains in heating oil, as it rose in sympathy with gas oil futures on London's IPE.
Dec gas oil, the European equivalent of heating oil, ended $3.00 a tonne higher at $221.50 as snow descended on parts of Europe.
Meanwhile, the National Weather Service's six to 10 day forecast called for temperatures to be below normal in the Northeast and Midwest.
Weather Services Corp forecasted temperatures to be up to eight degrees below normal this week and colder still into the weekend.

Dealers expected the American Petroleum Institute (API) to report that distillate stocks, which includes heating oil, fell for the week ended November 15 due to the cold spell. The API releases its weekly oil inventory report Tuesday evening.
Distillate inventories are low, with heating oil stocks a lean 14.5 million barrels below year ago.
Chartists were unsure whether heating oil could extend its gains Wednesday, as nearby heating oil closed near 74.00 cents, a heavy shelf of resistance.
"Tomorrow is going to tell the story," said Jake Bernstein, president of MBH Commodity Advisors in Illinois, adding he doubted whether resistance will be broken.
"I think heating oil will open higher, but close lower," said Bernstein.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
